## Key structural points (Hansen’s outline)

1. **3:12–14** — Double denial of perfection (“not already… not already”) + race imagery: forget what is behind, strain toward what is ahead, press on to the prize of the upward call. Cuts against *both* perfectionism *and* libertinism.
2. **3:15–17** — Mature (*teleioi*) = those who share Paul’s attitude (humble not-yet + wholehearted pressing on); freedom on minor points (God will reveal); live up to what attained; fellow-imitators of Paul / keep eyes on those who walk as “we” do (Paul + team; Timothy, Epaphroditus).
3. **3:18–19** — Fork in the road: enemies of the cross (ethical divergence, not primarily theological denial); not best identified with the Judaizers of 3:2; libertine/self-indulgent, mind on earthly things; end is destruction; Paul weeps.
4. **3:20–21** — Causal “for” motivating imitation (3:17): heavenly *politeuma*; eagerly await Savior/Lord Jesus from heaven (imperial language subverted; Isaiah/Jewish titles supply meaning); transform body of humiliation to conformity with Christ’s glorious body by power that subjects all things; continuity of somatic existence; tension with 1:23 left unresolved; complete salvation story with 2:6–11; hymn-fragment hypothesis entertained but not proven.

## Claims

### C. Pressing On toward the Goal (3:12–14)

**F001.** Hansen: Paul’s passionate intention to know Christ does not itself make him perfect; considering everything loss for knowing Christ was only the *beginning* of a daily discipline of pressing on.
- Quote: “Paul knows that his passionate intention to know Christ does not in itself make him perfect. His decision to consider everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ was only the beginning of a daily discipline to press on toward the goal.”
- Locus: slice ll. 5–6; Phil 3:12–14 context.

**F002.** Hansen: Authenticity of faith cannot be measured only by intensity of initial decision; “Receiving Christ is a lifetime adventure.”
- Quote: “The authenticity of faith in Christ cannot be measured only by the intensity of one’s initial decision to receive Christ. Receiving Christ is a lifetime adventure.”
- Locus: slice ll. 6–7.

**F003.** Hansen: Paul’s race self-portrait is a double-edged sword against (a) moral perfectionism and (b) moral libertinism.
- Quote: “Paul’s description of his daily discipline of straining toward what is ahead serves as a double-edged sword. On the one hand, Paul is correcting an attitude of moral perfectionism… On the other hand, Paul is also correcting an attitude of moral libertinism…”
- Locus: slice ll. 7–9.

**F004.** Hansen: Denial of perfection contradicts Jewish Christians claiming perfection via membership in the Jewish people, and perfectionists in every age promising “instant perfection.”
- Quote: “His denial of perfectionism contradicts not only those Jewish Christians in his day who were claiming and promising perfection by way of membership in the Jewish people, but also perfectionists in every age who are advertising their procedures as the way to procure instant perfection.”
- Locus: slice ll. 8–9; note 156.

**F005.** Hansen: Paul’s pressing on counters many who live as enemies of the cross (3:18–19: god = stomach, glory in shame, mind on earthly things).
- Quote: “Paul offers his example to counter many who live as enemies of the cross …: their god is their stomach, their glory is in their shame, and their mind is on earthly things (3:27-19).”
- Locus: slice ll. 9–10 (print ref garbled as 3:27–19 = 3:18–19).

**F006.** Hansen: Pagan cultural pressures dampen Christian determination; many gave up commitment to Christ and fell into popular immorality; Paul seeks to inspire them back into the race.
- Quote: “The pressures of the surrounding pagan culture dampen and even extinguish the enthusiasm and determination of Christians to press on to maturity… Many succumbed to these pressures, gave up their commitment to Christ, and fell back into the popular immorality of their culture.”
- Locus: slice ll. 10–11.

**F007.** Hansen: Race imagery cuts both ways: perfectionists who claim arrival and libertines who dropped out are both called back on track.
- Quote: “Paul’s dramatic imagery of his race cuts both ways: perfectionists who claim to have already arrived at the goal and libertines who have dropped out of the race are both called to get back on track and press on.”
- Locus: slice ll. 11–12.

**F008.** Hansen on 3:12: Double “not already” — still running, not at finish line; Greek lacks object for “obtained”; plausible sense is enter close relationship / apprehend; object may be Christ — Paul has not already fully apprehended Christ.
- Quote: “A plausible meaning of this verb in this context is ‘to enter into a close relationship, receive, make one’s own, apprehend /comprehend.’ This meaning supports the suggestion that Christ is the object of the verb: Paul has not already fully apprehended Christ.”
- Locus: slice ll. 13–14.

**F009.** Hansen: Intensified form of same verb: desire to take hold of that for which Christ took hold of Paul; ever since grasped by Christ, Paul desires to grasp/comprehend Christ; knowing Christ’s incomprehensible greatness demands a lifetime of arduous inquiry.
- Quote: “Ever since Paul was grasped and apprehended by Christ, he has desired to grasp and comprehend Christ. But ‘to know the incomprehensible greatness of Christ demands a lifetime of arduous in quirt'’”
- Locus: slice ll. 14–15.

**F010.** Hansen: Desire to gain Christ / be found in him (3:8–9) and know Christ (3:10) is a dynamic process of intellectual apprehension and moral transformation.
- Quote: “Paul’s desire to gain Christ and be found in him (3:8-9) and to know Christ (3:1o) engages him in an intimate relationship with Christ that is a dynamic process of intellectual apprehension and moral transformation.”
- Locus: slice ll. 15–16.

**F011.** Hansen: Second denial = not already “become perfect”; only occurrence of that verb in Paul; adjective *teleios* ranges: highest standard, mature/full-grown, fully developed morally, cult initiate (probably Phil 3:15; Col 1:28).
- Quote: “His first denial that he has already fully grasped Christ leads to his second denial that he has ‘already become perfect.’… the cognate adjective ‘perfect’ occurs seven times with a range of meanings… and ‘being a cult initiate’ (probably Phil 3:15; Col 1:28).”
- Locus: slice ll. 17–18.

**F012.** Hansen: 1 Cor 13:10–12 parallel — present partial knowledge vs future full knowledge face to face; Phil 3:12 denial is of same kind: not yet fully grasped Christ → not yet perfect; perfection only on day of Christ by Christ’s power (points ahead to 3:20–21).
- Quote: “precisely because he has not yet already fully grasped Christ, he has not already become perfect. Only when he sees Christ face to face will he be totally transformed by Christ’s power to be like him (3:20-21). Paul anticipates that he will become perfect in the ‘future-eschatological’ sense, but only on the day of Christ and by the power of Christ.”
- Locus: slice ll. 18–20.

**F013.** Hansen: Imperfection does not discourage pursuit; adversative “but” — incompleteness *compels* pressing on; *press on* = move rapidly and decisively toward an objective; same word as persecuting zeal (3:6) — formerly pursued church, now pursues Christ.
- Quote: “Rather than causing him to give up and quit, Paul’s sense of incompleteness compels him to press on.… Previously, his zeal for the law drove him to run after and pursue the church. Now he is running after and pursuing Christ, to know Christ.”
- Locus: slice ll. 21–22.

**F014.** Hansen: Ultimate reason for pursuit is Christ’s apprehension of Paul — “because I was apprehended by Christ”; Christ will not let go; divine grace is source and goal of human pursuit.
- Quote: “The ultimate reason for Paul’s pursuit of the apprehension of Christ is Christ’s apprehension of Paul: ‘because I was apprehended by Christ.’… Divine grace is the source and goal of the human pursuit.”
- Locus: slice ll. 22–24.

**F015.** Hansen on 3:13: Emphatic denial repeated; “brothers and sisters” = familial address stressing importance; *consider* = careful thought / rational self-assessment, not emotional upset.
- Quote: “The verb consider indicates that his admission of imperfection is not the result of an emotional upset or chronic melancholy. It means ‘to give careful thought to a matter’… After a careful assessment of himself, Paul draws a perfectly rational conclusion: I have not yet taken hold of it.”
- Locus: slice ll. 25–26.

**F016.** Hansen: “I myself” emphasizes personal self-evaluation and contrasts others who consider themselves perfect / already at apex.
- Quote: “Apparently, others consider themselves to be perfect; in their self-assessment, they are totally satisfied with themselves and confident that they have already arrived at the apex of human achievement.”
- Locus: slice ll. 26–27.

**F017.** Hansen: Third use of “take hold of” combines “win, attain” and “understand, comprehend”; object (not supplied by Paul) is knowledge of / relationship with Christ; not yet complete conformity to Christ’s obedience unto death, nor full understanding of Christ.
- Quote: “He has not yet attained to complete conformity to the standard of Christ’s obedience unto death on the cross, nor has he completely understood the full significance of Christ.”
- Locus: slice ll. 27–28.

**F018.** Hansen: “But one thing!” — elliptical; highest priority captivates full attention; all else secondary.
- Quote: “The highest priority in his life captivates his full attention and demands total concentration.… All his thoughts, emotions, and decisions are focused on this fixed point: One thing!”
- Locus: slice ll. 29–30.

**F019.** Hansen: Two parallel participles — forgetting what is behind / straining toward what is ahead — portray runner refusing to look back, every fiber forward.
- Quote: “These two clauses give a dramatic portrayal of a runner who refuses to look back over his shoulder, but keeps straining every fiber of his being forward toward the goal.”
- Locus: slice ll. 31.

**F020.** Hansen: “What is behind” in this context = things in life *as a believer* — achievements, attainments already achieved in walk with Christ (not primarily pre-conversion only); for ≥20 years of knowing/serving Christ he could claim arrival but instead forgets past achievements.
- Quote: “But Paul’s reference in this context to what is behind points to those things in his life as a believer in Christ.… What is behind is everything that he has already achieved and attained in his walk with Christ.”
- Locus: slice ll. 31–33.

**F021.** Hansen: Forgetting is not passive amnesia (letters full of past references) but active, continuous discipline — disregard, reject, nonobservance of past achievements as dwelling-place of the mind.
- Quote: “Forgetting is not a passive loss of memory; no, it is an active, continuous discipline of the mind and heart.… Although he did not actually forget the past, he emphatically chose to disregard it.”
- Locus: slice ll. 33–34.

**F022.** Hansen: *Straining* (hapax in NT) = exert oneself to the uttermost; runner bent forward, hand outstretched, eye on goal.
- Quote: “This is the only time this word straining appears in the NT. This verb means to ‘exert oneself to the uttermost.’”
- Locus: slice ll. 35–36 (slice numbering continues in prose block ~19–20 of read).

**F023.** Hansen: Self-portrait refutes perfectionism *and* resists turn from perfectionism to hedonism; temptation to drop out and “enjoy life” sets mind on earthly things (3:19); faith is running, not mere past decision or static state.
- Quote: “While Paul clearly refutes perfectionism in his self-portrait, at the same time he also resists the trend to turn from perfectionism to hedonism.… Faith is not simply a decision in the past or a static state of existence; faith is running a race, straining toward what is ahead.”
- Locus: slice ~ll. 35–36 (body of §13).

**F024.** Hansen on 3:14: Forgetting and straining modify *I press on* (manner); goal = mark/target; content of goal not specifically defined, but concentration on finish line is the point.
- Quote: “Although the actual content of the goal is not specifically defined by Paul, the image of the goal carries forward the thrust of Paul’s point: running the race of faith in Christ demands concentration on the finish line.”
- Locus: slice §14 opening.

**F025.** Hansen: Finish line could be being with Christ at death (1:23) *or* return of Christ from heaven (3:20); either way, run well to the end; half-race then sidelines is not an option.
- Quote: “Whether the finish line is being with Christ at death, as Paul contemplates in 1:23 (to depart and be with Christ), or the return of Christ from heaven, as Paul envisions in 3:20 (we eagerly await a Savior from there), Paul is determined to run the race well all the way to the finish line.”
- Locus: slice §14.

**F026.** Hansen: Prize imagery from Hellenistic games (“award for exceptional performance”); cf. 1 Cor 9:24; Paul precludes meriting the prize by asserting God’s heavenward call in Christ Jesus.
- Quote: “Paul precludes any illusion that his own performance merits the prize by asserting that God has called me heavenward in Christ Jesus. All of Paul’s strenuous effort responds to and is empowered by the gracious initiative of God’s ca1L.”
- Locus: slice §14.

**F027.** Hansen on genitive “prize of the upward call”: rejects genitive of apposition (prize = the call) because call is technical for God’s act bringing into fellowship with Christ (beginning of race, not end).
- Quote: “If this is a genitive of apposition, then the prize is the upward call of God. The difficulty with this definition of call is that it places the reception of the call in the future.… The call of God stands at the beginning, not the end, of the race that Paul runs.”
- Locus: slice §14 mid.

**F028.** Hansen: Also rejects overstated games-imagery reading (judge calling winner up) as understating theological content of *call* in Paul.
- Quote: “But this definition of call overstates its cultural connotations and understates its theological content in Paul’s letters.”
- Locus: slice §14.

**F029.** Hansen’s preferred reading: attainment of prize (being with Christ at end) is fulfillment of God’s call at beginning; genitive of *call* as subjective genitive — God’s call gives promise of the prize; effectual calling through gospel.
- Quote: “The attainment of the prize of being with Christ at the end of the race is the fulfillment of God’s call at the beginning of the race.… If God’s call is the invitation to press on toward the prize of communion with Christ, then the genitive case of call is a subjective genitive: God’s call gives believers the promise of the prize.”
- Locus: slice §14 late.

**F030.** Hansen: “Heavenward” = direction *and* origin of call — calling from above and to heavenly reward; Paul’s Damascus encounter = call from above; lifelong press toward prize of being with / knowing Christ free from earthly limitations.
- Quote: “The word heavenward indicates both the direction of the call and the origin of the call. God’s call is a calling from above and a calling to a heavenly reward.”
- Locus: slice §14 end.

### D. Mentoring Others (3:15–17)

**F031.** Hansen: Paul’s self-portrait is consistently Christ-centered (past reevaluation 3:4–9; present conformity 3:10; future prize 3:11–14); now directs Philippians to “take such a view of things,” join in following his example, align with those who live as he does.
- Quote: “His Christ-centered vision determines the way that he views his past, his present, and his future. Now Paul directs the Philippian church to take such a view of things.”
- Locus: slice § D intro (ll. 35–39 of slice file).

**F032.** Hansen: Apparent contradiction — v. 12 denies becoming perfect (*teleioō*) / v. 15 claims *teleioi* (“perfect/mature”) — resolved by historical context of opponents’ perfectionism via Jewish assimilation (circumcision/law); Paul turns perfectionism on its head: “what characterizes perfection is not to consider oneself perfect.”
- Quote: “Now he turns the entire concept of perfectionism on its head by asserting that ‘what characterizes perfection is not to consider oneself perfect.’ Christian perfection ‘consists, stated paradoxically, in Christian imperfection, in running towards the goal.’”
- Locus: slice §15.

**F033.** Hansen: In this context *teleioi* = mature; maturity = taking Paul’s view/attitude/way of thinking as just expressed.
- Quote: “In this context, Paul defines the meaning of the word teleioi as mature.… Maturity is taking Paul’s view of things, having Paul’s attitude, and adopting Paul’s way of thinking.”
- Locus: slice §15.

**F034.** Hansen: “Let us have this attitude” links to 2:5 (Christ’s attitude); practical path to Christ’s attitude is Paul’s attitude; Paul’s loss-for-Christ (3:7–8) reflects Christ’s self-emptying / obedience to death (2:7–8).
- Quote: “When Paul decided to consider everything a loss because of the surpassing knowledge of knowing Christ (3:7-8), his attitude reflected that of the one who made himself nothing, … humbled himself and was obedient unto death - even death on the cross! (2:7-8).”
- Locus: slice §15.

**F035.** Hansen: Mature attitude = genuine humility (not already arrived) + wholehearted commitment (straining toward goal); first-person plural calls for unity of mind (cf. 2:2), not individualistic competitive racing.
- Quote: “The mature attitude exhibited by Paul combines genuine humility, knowing that we have not already arrived at the goal, and wholehearted commitment, straining toward the goal.… This attitude draws people together as they focus in their community on knowing Christ and following Christ.”
- Locus: slice §15.

**F036.** Hansen: Paul draws together “friends of the cross” before referring to “enemies of the cross” (3:18).
- Quote: “He is drawing together the friends of the cross before he refers to the enemies of the cross (3:18).”
- Locus: slice §15.

**F037.** Hansen on “if on some point you think differently”: *think* twice stresses same attitude on major principles; difference only on some *point* — not essential differences like enemies of the cross (vv. 18–19); no total uniformity coerced; God will make clear.
- Quote: “Paul is not referring here to essential differences such as he addresses in his description of the enemies of the cross of Christ in verses i8- 19.… Without any sign of anxiety or resentment, he allows his readers freedom… with the assurance that God will make clear to them how to handle their differences.”
- Locus: slice §15 late.

**F038.** Hansen: Means of God’s revelation left undefined/open; move from law-centered life frees from Mishnah-like detailed prescriptions; true unity by God’s revelation, not rhetorical power.
- Quote: “How God will reveal his direction to resolve minor points of difference Paul does not explain. He seems content to leave the means of God’s guidance undefined and open.… true unity will be achieved only by God’s revelation, not by his rhetorical power.”
- Locus: slice §15 end; echoes 1:6; 2:13.

**F039.** Hansen on 3:16: “Only let us live up to what we have already attained” — positive appreciation; they have reached a level setting high standard; “be in line with” standard of progress so far (cf. Gal 5:25; 6:16 keep in step).
- Quote: “The verb attained signifies that they have already arrived at a point in their journey and reached a level of understanding and conduct in their faith that sets a high standard for their future belief and behavior.”
- Locus: slice §16.

**F040.** Hansen: Not criticizing lack of progress or coercing new direction; call is to live up to own experience of God’s work (2:13); “no extravagances to right or to left.”
- Quote: “These believers are not being forced to conform to some standard outside themselves; they are being called to live up to their own experience of God’s gracious work in their community…”
- Locus: slice §16.

**F041.** Hansen: First-person plural — corporate partnership attainment (1:5; 2:1; participation in Christ’s sufferings 3:10), not individualistic; threatened by selfish ambition (1:17; 2:3); maintained by humility of Christ (2:8) and of Paul (3:8–10).
- Quote: “An in dividualistic understanding of what we have already attained does not do justice to Paul’s theme of the attainment of the community as a whole in their experience and expression of partnership in the gospel.”
- Locus: slice §16 end.

**F042.** Hansen on 3:17: Paul’s example imperfect yet tangible/accessible; mentor role: “Join together in following my example”; literally “fellow imitators of me” — compound unattested elsewhere, possibly Paul’s coinage.
- Quote: “Literally, Paul calls them to become ‘fellow imitators of me.’ The compound word ‘fellow imitators’ is not attested elsewhere in Greek literature and may be Paul’s own creation.”
- Locus: slice §17.

**F043.** Hansen: Phrase could mean fellow imitators *with* Paul *of Christ*; whole letter stresses mutuality/equality; joining Paul = common pursuit of “one thing” (3:13) = know Christ / power of resurrection / sufferings / death (3:10).
- Quote: “When they are fellow imitators of Paul, they will be united in their common pursuit of one thing (3:13): to know Christ - yes, to know the power of his resurrection and participation in his sufferings, becoming like him in his death (3:10).”
- Locus: slice §17.

**F044.** Hansen *rejects* readings of imitation call as defense of apostleship or as constructing hierarchy Christ–Paul–Christians; that turns self-portrait upside down — loss of privilege for Christ; imitating Paul = way to imitate Christ (2:5–8 way of the cross).
- Quote: “To view Paul’s call to be fellow imitators of his example as a ‘defense of his own apostleship’ or as a way to construct and enforce ‘the hierarchy, Christ-Paul-Christians’ turns Paul’s entire self-portrait in this chapter upside down.… Imitating Paul is the way to imitate Christ.”
- Locus: slice §17.

**F045.** Hansen: Also “keep your eyes on those who live as we do” — careful attention to other examples; Timothy and Epaphroditus (2:19–30) exemplify self-giving service; ethical term is “walk” (not merely TNIV “live”).
- Quote: “Timothy and Epaphroditus represent the kind of people Paul has in mind (2:19-30).… Although TNIV uses the term live, Paul uses his favorite ethical term for Christian behavior: those who ‘walk.’”
- Locus: slice §17 mid.

**F046.** Hansen: OT “walk” (Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Psalms) and Halakah background; purpose not detailed legal application but personal relationships with mentors modeling walk with Jesus Christ.
- Quote: “His purpose is not to set forth a detailed application of law, but to encourage the development of personal relationships with mentors who model the way to walk with Jesus Christ.”
- Locus: slice §17.

**F047.** Hansen: “Us” as model — may be Paul alone, but given Timothy/Epaphroditus and 4:3 co-workers, plural “probably refers to Paul and his team of associates”; model = archetype for Christian moral life.
- Quote: “his first person plural probably ‘refers to Paul and his team of associates.’… This model serves as an ‘archetype’ for the moral life of Christians.”
- Locus: slice §17 end.

### E. Mourning over the Enemies of the Cross (3:18–19)

**F048.** Hansen: Opposition of two “walks” — fork in road: Christ-centered vs self-centered life; warning against dominant cultural fashions opposed to the cross.
- Quote: “By repeating the verb ‘walk’ (TNIV, live), Paul places a fork in the road. We must make a radical choice between two different ways to live: the Christ-centered life or the self-centered life.”
- Locus: slice § E intro / §18.

**F049.** Hansen: Conjunction “for” connects warning to 3:17 imperative — close adherence to positive examples necessary because negative examples allure toward destruction.
- Quote: “The conjunction for connects this warning to the previous command, keep your eyes on those who live as we do, and gives the reason for that command.”
- Locus: slice §18.

**F050.** Hansen: Enemies not addressed as letter recipients (outside holy people in Christ at Philippi) but their influence is strong; warning often repeated; now “even with tears.”
- Quote: “Paul does not speak directly to the many people who live as enemies of the cross; they are not included with God’s holy people in Christ Jesus at Philippi (1:1)… their influence on the community is so strong that Paul frequently repeats his warning.”
- Locus: slice §18.

**F051.** Hansen: Enemies unnamed — escape definitive identification; *some* commentators identify with Judaizers of 3:2 (dogs, mutilators), rereading stomach/shame/earthly as food laws, circumcision, ethnic privileges.
- Quote: “Some commentators see signs of Jewish Christians in Paul’s description of them.… if Paul is thinking of Judaizers again… since they are preoccupied with food laws, their god is their stomach; since they exalt the importance of circumcision, their glory is in their shame; since they focus on their ethnic Jewish privileges, their mind is set on earthly things.”
- Locus: slice §18 mid (position of others, not Hansen’s preferred ID).

**F052.** Hansen *rejects* Judaizer identification for 3:18–19: difficulties = no clear connection of Jewish food laws with idolatry in Paul; no evidence Paul viewed circumcision/male genitals as shameful; Paul does not dismiss Jewish privileges as “earthly things”; he can approve food-law observance in circumstances, circumcision of Jews as law-faithfulness sign, and lists privileges as irrevocable gifts (Rom 9:4–5; 11:29).
- Quote: “The difficulties faced by this interpretation, however, are the absence of any clear connection between Jewish food laws and idolatry in Paul’s letters, the absence of any evidence that Paul viewed circumcision or male genitals as shameful, and the absence of Paul’s dismissal of Jewish privileges as earthly things.”
- Locus: slice §18 late.

**F053.** Hansen’s preferred ID: focus on *how they live/walk*; problem is ethical divergence from the way of the cross, *not* theological denial of the cross; cross narrative = humility, servant, obedience unto death (2:7–8); framed by anti–selfish ambition (2:3) and work out salvation (2:12); Paul’s renunciation (3:4–10) exemplifies walking the cross-way.
- Quote: “The problem with these people is not a theological denial of the cross of Christ, but an ethical divergence from the way of the cross of Christ.… In this context, enemies of the cross are those who ‘seek to avoid suffering that might come their way as the result of their convictions about Christ.’ Their selfish ambitions are opposed to the way of the cross.”
- Locus: slice §18 end.

**F054.** Hansen: Paul speaks weeping; such outpouring reserved for those who professed belief in Christ; third-person outsiders yet close to heart; pastoral mourning — harsh words, broken heart.
- Quote: “When Paul speaks of these people who are walking contrary to the way of the cross of Christ in their pursuit of their own self-interests, he speaks with tears.… Paul reserves such an outpouring of emotion for those who have professed belief in Christ.… Though his words are harsh, his heart is broken. He mourns over the enemies of the cross.”
- Locus: slice §18 end / transition to §19.

**F055.** Hansen on 3:19 wordplay: mature (*teleioi*) vs destiny/end (*telos*) = destruction; enemies think they arrived at *telos*/perfection elevating them above suffering; true *teleioi* admit not arrived (3:12) and participate in Christ’s sufferings (1:29; 3:10); deliberate refusal to suffer with Christ separates from salvation.
- Quote: “In a play on words, Paul contrasts all of us who are mature (teleioi) with the enemies of the cross, whose destiny (telos) is destruction.… In their deliberate refusal to suffer with Christ, they have separated themselves from salvation in Christ.”
- Locus: slice §19 opening.

**F056.** Hansen: Self-indulgence in appetites, pride, mind — “god is their stomach,” “glory is in their shame,” “mind set on earthly things”; *stomach* metaphorically seat of desires; Rom 16:18; 1 Cor 6:13 — unbridled sensuality (gluttony or sexual licentiousness); worship of appetites.
- Quote: “These passages indicate that Paul uses the term stomach to represent ‘unbridled sensuality, whether gluttony or sexual licentiousness.’ For those who have no higher authority for the way they live than the dictates of their bodily appetites, their god is their stomach. They worship their appetites.”
- Locus: slice §19.

**F057.** Hansen: “Glory in their shame” — broadcast/brag about shameful indulgence; shame may allude to sexual immorality (Rom 1:27; Rev 3:18); modern analogy to celebrity media fame via shameful acts.
- Quote: “these people take pride in their shame; they broadcast and brag about their shameful indulgence of their physical appetites… Paul’s reference to people who ‘find their glory in that which causes them shame’ sounds strangely similar to media coverage of celebrities made famous by their shameful acts.”
- Locus: slice §19.

**F058.** Hansen: Root = mind set on earthly things; same *phroneō* verb as 2:2, 2:5, 3:15, 4:2 (Christ-centered unity) now depicts self-centered divisive obsession with earthly gratification; contrast heavenward call (3:14).
- Quote: “People with this orientation of life are obsessed with getting earthly things for their own personal gratification.… In contrast to pursuing the heavenward call of God in Christ Jesus (3:14), they are concentrating on their earthly possessions and pleasures.”
- Locus: slice §19.

**F059.** Hansen: These people had *probably been members* of the Philippian Christian community; now “turned full circle; having abandoned the way of the cross, they have their mind once again set on earthly things.”
- Quote: “These people had probably been members of the Christian community in Philippi, but now they ‘have turned full circle; having abandoned the way of the cross, they have their mind once again set on earthly things.’”
- Locus: slice §19 late.

**F060.** Hansen: 3:18–19 antithesis to 3:17 imitation call; no middle ground — stomach-god vs knowing Christ; earthly things vs heavenward call; cf. Luke 16:13 cannot serve two masters.
- Quote: “Paul does not offer any middle ground or middle way.… Either their god is their stomach or they will consider everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (3:7).”
- Locus: slice §19 end.

---

### Expecting Christ’s Ultimate Victory (3:20–21) — *politeuma*, Savior, body

**F061.** Hansen: Turn from earthly-minded (3:19) to citizenship in heaven (3:20); lyrical uniting of present heavenly citizenship with ultimate victory of Savior Lord Jesus Christ.
- Quote: “In these lyrical lines, Paul unites a proclamation of our present citizenship in the heavenly commonwealth with an announcement of the ultimate victory of our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.”
- Locus: slice §20 intro.

**F062.** Hansen: Emphatic “our” contrasts earthly- and heavenly-minded; most translations insert adversative “but,” but Paul uses causal “for” connecting to imperatives of v. 17; translators rightly mark contrast with enemies (3:18–19) but miss explanatory function as reason to obey 3:17.
- Quote: “Although most translations insert the adversative conjunction but… Paul’s use of the causal conjunction ‘for’ connects this sentence with the imperatives of verse 17.… translators accurately point to the contrast… but they miss the explanatory function of this sentence as a compelling reason to follow the imperatives in 3:17.”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F063.** Hansen’s structure: two imperatives (3:17) + two motivating reasons — (1) dark picture: earthly-minded → destruction; (2) radiant picture: heavenly citizenship → Savior’s return and bodily transformation; eschatology grounds ethics.
- Quote: “Paul seeks to motivate his readers to imitate him and those who walk like him by painting two pictures… Paul’s eschatological vision establishes the basis for his ethical imperatives. The future shines a bright light on the present to guide our moral choices.”
- Locus: slice §20 (structure table referenced).

**F064.** Hansen: Already citizens of heavenly order; not wishful thinking; based on righteousness from God — by God’s judicial decision believers belong to heavenly community.
- Quote: “From Paul’s eschatological perspective, we are already citizens of the heavenly order of reality. Our citizenship in heaven is not based upon wishful thinking or an imagination of future possibilities, but on the righteousness that comes from God. The righteousness that comes from God means that by God’s judicial decision we belong to the heavenly community.”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F065.** Hansen on *politeuma* (citizenship): connotes active constitutive force regulating citizens; by extension state and citizens under sovereign government; Aristotle: government (*politeuma*) everywhere sovereign in the state; Paul emphasizes membership in heavenly kingdom governed by Christ — “Our governing power, our executive authority is in heaven.”
- Quote: “The term citizenship (politeuma) connotes an active, ‘constitutive force regulating its citizens.’… Paul’s use of the word emphasizes the membership of Christians in the heavenly kingdom governed by Christ. Our governing power, our executive authority is in heaven.”
- Locus: slice §20 (load-bearing *politeuma*).

**F066.** Hansen: Implication = “colony of heavenly citizens” on earth; metaphor of foreigners pledging allegiance to home government / exile.
- Quote: “The implication of asserting our citizenship in the heavenly state is that we are a ‘colony of heavenly citizens’ here on earth. This concept of belonging to a community of foreigners who pledge allegiance to the government in their home country became a metaphor for living in exile.”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F067.** Hansen: Josephus — Diaspora Jews in Alexandria as commonwealth (*politeuma*); final authority of Jerusalem law-interpreters though residing in Alexandria. Philo — Platonic *politeuma* as heavenly realm of virtues/ideas. Such Jewish metaphorical uses *may* have influenced Paul.
- Quote: “Josephus referred to the community of Diaspora Jews in Alexandria as a commonwealth (politeuma).… Philo… used the term politeuma as a reference to the heavenly realm of virtues and ideas.… These Jewish metaphorical applications of the term politeuma may have influenced Paul’s assertion that Christians belong to a heavenly community.”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F068.** Hansen: *Perhaps* Jewish Christian opponents (cf. 3:2) claimed *politeuma* for their authority — but contest with Jewish claims is *not* Paul’s primary concern here.
- Quote: “Perhaps, Paul’s Jewish Christian opponents (see 3:2) claimed the term as their own to assert their authority. But a contest with Jewish claims or Jewish-Christian opponents does not appear to be the primary concern of Paul’s language here.”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F069.** Hansen (primary contextual load): special significance for church in *Roman colony Philippi* — Augustus conferred Roman constitutional rights; equal footing with Italian cities; official language Latin; majority of inscriptions Latin confirm Roman orientation. Contrast: Roman Philippians’ *politeuma* in Rome vs Christians’ *politeuma* in heaven.
- Quote: “His terminology carries special significance for the church in the Roman colony called Philippi.… In contrast to the allegiance of Roman Philippians to their governing power, their politeuma, in Rome, Paul sets forth the parallel and opposing claim of Christians that their governing power, their politeuma, is in heaven.”
- Locus: slice §20 end (load-bearing colonial contrast).

**F070.** Hansen: Sharper focus in next phrase — “we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ.” In empire, Caesar Augustus acclaimed “savior of the world” for order/peace; Paul’s “Savior” in letter to Roman Philippi “sharply opposes Jesus Christ as Lord to the imperial savior.”
- Quote: “In the Roman Empire, Caesar Augustus was acclaimed to be the ‘savior of the world’… Paul’s use of the term Savior in his letter to Christians in Roman Philippi ‘sharply opposes Jesus Christ as Lord to the imperial savior.’”
- Locus: slice §20–21 transition (load-bearing imperial language).

**F071.** Hansen: Applying imperial title Savior to Jesus — Paul “explicitly (and we must assume deliberately) speaks of Jesus in language which echoes, and hence deeply subverts, language in common use among Roman imperial subjects to describe Caesar.” Redirect from savior in Rome (Caesar) to Savior in heaven (Jesus Christ the Lord).
- Quote: “By applying the imperial title Savior to Jesus Christ, ‘Paul explicitly (and we must assume deliberately) speaks of Jesus in language which echoes, and hence deeply subverts, language in common use among Roman imperial subjects to describe Caesar.’ Paul redirects the focus of his readers from the savior in Rome, Caesar Augustus, to the Savior in heaven, Jesus Christ the Lord.”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F072.** Hansen: Enemies of the cross followed natural Philippian inclination to look to emperor in Rome for power, appetites, rescue, protection; those following Paul’s example look to Jesus as Lord and Savior — change of allegiance inevitably entails participation in Christ’s sufferings (3:10); hope fixed on Jesus not Caesar.
- Quote: “The enemies of the cross followed the natural inclination of residents in Philippi to look to the emperor in Rome… But the Christian who followed the example of Paul (3:17) looked to Jesus Christ to be their Lord and Savior. Such a change of allegiance would inevitably cause them to participate in the sufferings of Christ (3:10).”
- Locus: slice §20.

**F073.** Hansen: Though Caesar’s titles “savior” and “lord” used to subvert undivided allegiance to Caesar, *meaning* of titles comes from Jewish heritage — especially Isaiah 45:15, 21–23 (already OT backdrop of Christ hymn Phil 2:9–11); lifelong Jewish conviction God alone is Savior and Lord; applied to Jesus: Jesus, not Caesar, rightful bearer of divine titles; trusted as Savior, worshipped as Lord.
- Quote: “Although Paul uses Caesar’s titles ‘savior’ and ‘lord’ for Jesus in this context in order to subvert the use of these titles in the Roman Empire as an expression of absolute, undivided allegiance to Caesar, Paul’s Jewish heritage provides the meaning for these titles. Especially significant is the use of these titles in the text of Isaiah 45:15, 21-23, already observed as the OT backdrop of the Christ hymn (Phil 2:9-11)… Jesus, not Caesar, is the rightful bearer of the divine titles, Savior and Lord.”
- Locus: slice §20 late (Isaiah + imperial double register).

**F074.** Hansen: *Eagerly await* = ultimate eschatological hope vocabulary across Paul (Gal 5:5; Rom 8:19, 23; 1 Cor 1:7); Phil 3:20 first-person plural — whole community as community of hope; unites all with Paul’s 3:13–14 orientation; present suffering still dominated by hope.
- Quote: “By using the first person plural we eagerly await a Savior (Phil 3:21), Paul characterizes the whole Christian community as a community of hope… Even though their present experience includes suffering, they are all still dominated by hope.”
- Locus: slice §20–21 (note: Hansen’s parenthetical “3:21” for the verb phrase appears in slice; verb is in 3:20).

**F075.** Hansen: Contrast of hopes — earthly agenda hopes for earthly savior (Caesar visiting colony from mother city Rome bringing order/peace); Christian hope echoes imperial eschatology’s titles but Savior comes *from heaven, not from Rome*.
- Quote: “Although the eschatological hope of the Christian community echoes the imperial eschatology with its use of Caesar’s titles, Savior and Lord, the Savior and Lord anticipated by the Christian community is corning from heaven, not from Rome.”
- Locus: slice §20 end.

**F076.** Hansen on 3:21: Political overtones continue — share glory of Savior and universal subjugation; Caesar no match for heavenly Savior/Lord; written from Roman prison to Roman colony — greater future vision than any Caesar.
- Quote: “No matter how glorious Caesar is or how great the power of his rule over all things in his empire, Caesar is no match for the Savior and Lord from heaven. Writing from a Roman prison to a Roman colony, Paul spells out a greater vision of the future than any Caesar could ever accomplish.”
- Locus: slice §21 opening.

**F077.** Hansen: *Transform* = dramatic supernatural change of form of body from lowly to glorious; present = “body of humiliation”; future like his glorious body; “humiliation” = unpretentious state/condition of present bodily experience.
- Quote: “The verb transform envisions a dramatic, supernatural event when Christ will ‘change the form’ of our body from lowly to glo- rious.… By defining the lowly form of our present body in terms of ‘humiliation,’ Paul points to the ‘unpretentious state or condition’ of our present bodily experience.”
- Locus: slice §21.

**F078.** Hansen: Though body can be “body of sin” / “body of death,” Paul expresses no Gnostic/dualist contempt for body as inherently corrupt/evil; body = outward physical expression of whole person (sinful desires or Spirit’s directions).
- Quote: “he does not express Gnostic or dualist contempt for the body, as if the body itself were inherently corrupt and evil. The body is the outward, physical expression of the whole person…”
- Locus: slice §21.

**F079.** Hansen: “Humiliation” echoes Christ hymn — Christ humbled himself (2:7–8); Christ experienced humiliation in incarnation; present bodily life filled with weakness, suffering, death; prison chains and imminent execution = Paul’s personal humiliation; brutally realistic portrait without airbrushing.
- Quote: “The term ‘humiliation’ echoes the use of the verb ‘humbled’ in the Christ hymn.… Writing from prison, Paul is acutely aware that his chains and his imminent execution are elements of his personal humiliation.… Paul paints a brutally realistic portrait of our lowly bodies without any removal of blemishes or addition of halos.”
- Locus: slice §21.

**F080.** Hansen: Line of continuity = existence *in a body*; hope not rescue *from* body but body *transformed*; no contemplation of future out-of-body or bodiless human existence; Christian future as somatic as Christ’s bodily resurrection; redemption *of* bodies (Rom 8) and creation, not *from* creation; bodies changed, not discarded.
- Quote: “The line of continuity in our present and future forms of existence is existence in a body. Paul’s hope is not to be rescued from his body, but to have his body transformed; he does not contemplate a future out of the body or bodiless human existence.… Paul’s hope is not for redemption from creation but for the redemption of creation, including the redemption of our bodies. Our bodies will be changed, but not discarded.”
- Locus: slice §21 (resurrection-body continuity — load-bearing).

**F081.** Hansen: Continuity of somatic existence does not answer DNA/memory/personality questions; where Paul addresses continuity, seed–plant analogy (1 Cor 15:36–38) suggests “identity with a difference.”
- Quote: “Attempts to answer these and many related questions go beyond Paul’s simple assertion of a continuity of somatic existence.… The best we can say is that the seed analogy suggests a continuity of ‘identity with a difference.’”
- Locus: slice §21.

**F082.** Hansen on tension with 1:21–23: Emphasis on bodily continuity raises doubts Paul contemplated bodiless existence; yet “to die is gain” / “depart and be with Christ, better by far” — death as personal communion with Christ does *not* support cessation of personal existence (“sleep”) until parousia/resurrection.
- Quote: “Paul’s definition of death as personal communion with Christ does not support the view that there is a cessation of personal existence, euphemistically called sleep, until the return of Christ and the resurrection of the body. We cannot press Paul’s assertion that human existence means somatic existence so far that it denies Paul’s own expectation of personal communion with Christ at the time of death.”
- Locus: slice §21 (intermediate state).

**F083.** Hansen: Traditional resolution = intermediate state of bodiless soul — but this “radically conflicts with Paul’s expectation of a continuity of somatic human existence.” Other hypotheses: instantaneous resurrection at death; intermediate body before final resurrection. Paul does not hypothesize to resolve the conflict; unsolved mystery does not diminish eagerness for either being with Christ at death or bodily transformation.
- Quote: “The traditional way to resolve the tension… is the hypothesis of an intermediate state of bodiless human existence… But this hypothesis radically conflicts with Paul’s expectation of a continuity of somatic human existence. Other hypotheses include instantaneous resurrection of the body at the time of death or an intermediate body… Paul does not hypothesize to resolve the apparent conflict… But this unsolved mystery does not diminish his eagerness to be with Christ when he dies and his eagerness for his body to be transformed.”
- Locus: slice §21 (Hansen’s engagement — positions recorded, not adjudicated as wiki fact).

**F084.** Hansen: Radical discontinuity = humiliation vs glory; “conformed” = same form as Christ’s glorious body; Christ always perfect prototype — conformed to his death now (3:10), to glorious body future (3:21); risen body is “body of his glory.”
- Quote: “Christ is always the perfect prototype, the divine paradigm for Paul. He desires ‘to be conformed to his death’ in the present (3:10); he anticipates being ‘conformed to his glorious body’ in the future (3:21).”
- Locus: slice §21.

**F085.** Hansen: Via 1 Cor 15 — resurrection body “spiritual” = perfectly animated/guided by Spirit; incorruptible, glorious, powerful vs corruptible, dishonorable, weak natural body; Christians display likeness of risen Christ, last Adam, heavenly man.
- Quote: “The ‘spiritual body’ is a body perfectly ‘animated and guided by the spirit.’… In all of these characteristics of their resurrection bodies, Christians will display the likeness of the risen Christ, the last Adam, the heavenly man (1 Cor 1545-49).”
- Locus: slice §21.

**F086.** Hansen: Essential difference — Christ’s unrivaled power to transform bodies *by the power that enables him to bring everything under his control*; echoes Caesar’s claim over subjects’ bodies; Paul in chains by Caesar’s decree — only Christ subjects *all things*; earthly tyrants’ power to humiliate overcome when Christ subjects all and transforms bodies of humiliation; Christ not Caesar exercises universal dominion; echoes exaltation (2:9–11) and universal acclamation of Lord.
- Quote: “Here again Paul’s language echoes the claims of Caesar. The Roman emperors claim absolute power over the bodies of their subjects. Paul sits in chains by Caesar’s decree. But only Christ has the power to bring everything under his control.… Christ, not Caesar, will exercise universal dominion by his power… By the subjection of all things under his control Jesus Christ will deserve the universal acclamation that he alone is the Lord, far above all earthly powers.”
- Locus: slice §21 (exaltation-christology / *kyrios*).

**F087.** Hansen: Unites individual and cosmic transformation; reasoning cosmic → individual: power over universe entails power for personal transformation; personal transformation included within cosmic subjugation; may include process but future event cannot be replaced by historical process; weeping over those watching Caesar’s historical “gospel” of dominion; true gospel = Savior from heaven.
- Quote: “Paul’s reasoning is from the cosmic to the individual: since the Lord has the power to bring the entire universe under his control, he certainly has the power to accomplish our personal transformation.… While this future event may include some process, the future event cannot be replaced by historical process.”
- Locus: slice §21 late.

**F088.** Hansen: Pseudo-saviors seeking world dominion must not eclipse true Savior; even in Caesar’s prisons/chains, eagerly await Savior.
- Quote: “Paul does not allow the pseudo-saviors of the world to eclipse the true Savior who will come from heaven to exercise his sovereign power over all things and transform the humiliation of his people into glory. Even when we are locked in Caesar’s dark prisons and bound in Caesar’s chains, we eagerly await a Savior.”
- Locus: slice §21 end of main exposition.

### Parallels 2:6–11 // 3:20–21; hymn-fragment hypothesis

**F089.** Hansen: Combination of 2:6–11 and 3:20–21 tells complete salvation story through suffering to glory: eternal divine form (2:6) → incarnation (2:7) → cross (2:8) → exaltation / name above every name / every tongue confesses Lord (2:9–11) → coming from heaven to subject all things and transform lowly bodies like his glorious body (3:20–21).
- Quote: “A combination of 2:6-11 and 3:20-21 tells the complete story of the way of salvation that leads through suffering to glory.… In 3:20-21 the story announces the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ from heaven to bring everything under his control and transform our lowly bodies so that they will be like his glorious body.”
- Locus: slice closing synthesis.

**F090.** Hansen: Great “interchange” — Christ shared our suffering so we share his glory; became like us to transform us to become like him; story ends not in heaven but on earth — Savior comes from heaven to restore all creation.
- Quote: “The story of salvation tells us of a great ‘interchange’ between Christ and us: Christ came to share in our suffering so that we would share in his glory. He became like us in order to transform us to become like him. This story does not end in heaven, but on earth. The Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, comes from heaven to restore all of creation.”
- Locus: slice closing synthesis.

**F091.** Hansen: Because 3:20–21 is grand climax of salvation story, “this text seems to function as the final verse of the Christ hymn (2:6–11)”; remarkable verbal/conceptual parallels appear to confirm 3:20–21 belongs with the Christ hymn.
- Quote: “Since 3:20-21 announces the grand climax of the story of salvation, this text seems to function as the final verse of the Christ hymn (2:6-11). Re markable parallels between the words and concepts of the two passages appear to confirm that 3:20-21 belongs with the Christ hymn.”
- Locus: slice end (table of parallels alluded to but not fully reproduced in slice OCR).

**F092.** Hansen (hymn-fragment hypothesis — as scholarly position engagement, not asserted as settled fact): Unusual words in 3:20–21 rare/unattested elsewhere in Paul seem to confirm quoting early Christian hymn fragment; conjunction “for” and relative “who” seem to signal liturgical confession; **none of this evidence definitively proves** the pre-Pauline hymn hypothesis.
- Quote: “A number of unusual words in 3:20-21 not often or ever used elsewhere in Paul’s letters also seem to confirm that Paul is quoting a fragment of an early Christian hymn. In addition, the conjunction ‘for’ and the relative pronoun who appear to signal a ‘liturgical confession.’ None of this evidence definitively proves the hypothesis that 3:20-21 is a pre-Pauline Christian hymn.”
- Locus: slice final paragraph; notes 294–296.

**F093.** Hansen’s alternative: close connection with 2:6–11 may simply mean Paul’s heart reverberates with that hymn as he composes; image of Paul and Silas singing hymns in Philippian jail (Acts 16:25) and writing from Roman prison — hymns ringing through letter, lifting readers to envision humiliation transformed into participation in Christ’s complete victory.
- Quote: “The close connection of this passage with the Christ hymn (2:6-11) may simply indicate that Paul’s heart reverberates with the words and themes of that hymn as he composes these lines… Christian hymns of praise can be heard ringing through the lines of his letter and lifting his readers to envision a bright future when all the humiliation of suffering will be transformed to glorious participation in Christ’s complete victory over all things.”
- Locus: slice final paragraph.
